What should I ask before I call this asset detention, retention, or infiltration?

In 30 seconds

Start with the water, not the label. Identify what enters, where it can wait, every route it can leave, the objective the asset was built to serve, and the evidence needed to show that route still works.

Route the same storm

Where can the same stormwater go in each arrangement?

Route the same storm

EPA GUIDANCE AND TECHNICAL REFERENCE · pendingINSTRUCTIONAL · pending

The planned tracer uses one illustrative storm and three unlabeled physical arrangements. It reveals temporary storage and controlled release, permanent pool and displacement, infiltration, evapotranspiration, underdrain discharge, overflow, and bypass as separate routes. The values and routes are authored for instruction, not prediction.

Trace one storm through three water rooms

Reveal storage, release, infiltration, evapotranspiration, underdrain, overflow, and bypass as distinct pathways before showing common practice names.

Model boundary: Qualitative authored routes for instruction. No calibrated rainfall, runoff, hydraulic, infiltration, treatment, groundwater, flood, or compliance prediction.

03
Why do detention and retention seem to mean different things in different places?
Names are clues, not proof

Why do detention and retention seem to mean different things in different places?

Names are clues, not proof

SYNTHESIS PENDING QUALIFIED REVIEW · pendingEPA GUIDANCE AND TECHNICAL REFERENCE · pendingEPA TECHNICAL REFERENCE · pending

EPA sources use detention consistently for temporary storage and later release, but retention is used in more than one way. One source may mean runoff kept from later surface discharge. Another may mean a permanent pool that remains while new runoff displaces water. The brief will state the intended usage and show the physical route every time.

04
What changes when water crosses into soil or groundwater?
Infiltration crosses a boundary

What changes when water crosses into soil or groundwater?

Infiltration crosses a boundary

EPA GUIDANCE · pendingUS FEDERAL STATUTE · pending

The planned cutaway separates surface ponding, filter media, native soil, underdrain, seasonal groundwater, and receiving water. It teaches that captured water may infiltrate, filter, drain, overflow, or interact with groundwater depending on site and design. It does not supply a universal separation or infiltration criterion.

claim-green-infrastructure-definitionUNDER REVIEW · pending

Federal law defines green infrastructure as measures using plant or soil systems, permeable surfaces, stormwater harvest and reuse, or landscaping to store, infiltrate, or evapotranspirate stormwater and reduce flows to sewer systems or surface waters.

Research decision: pending

  • 33 USC 1362 Definitions, paragraph 27, Green InfrastructureUnited States Congress · us_federal_primary_authority · us governing or contextDefines green infrastructure. It does not define every local stormwater practice name or provide design criteria.

Limit: The definition does not specify design criteria or make every detention or retention asset green infrastructure.

claim-groundwater-protectionUNDER REVIEW · pending

Research decision: pending

Limit: The brief cannot determine suitability, separation, pretreatment, or groundwater risk for a real site.

What this brief can and cannot establish

EPA GUIDANCE · pendingUS FEDERAL REGULATION · pendingINSTRUCTIONAL · pending

This brief can teach a pathway-first way to ask better questions. It cannot determine an asset's design, capacity, drawdown, infiltration rate, treatment performance, groundwater suitability, maintenance action, or compliance. Those decisions require current drawings, site evidence, approved procedures, applicable permits, and qualified judgment.
